entities.name: Nicholas of Osimo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nicholas of Osimo (Niccolò da Osimo), an Italian Franciscan friar, jurist, and moral theologian, emerged as a pivotal figure in late medieval practical theology, dying in 1453, the very year Constantinople fell. His extensive body of work, particularly his influential *Supplementum Summae Pisanellae*, became a standard reference for confessors and preachers across Europe, shaping the pastoral practice of the Church for centuries. Operating within the Observant branch of the Franciscan order, Nicholas's writings synthesized complex theological and canonical principles into accessible guides for clerical use, bridging academic discourse with the everyday spiritual needs of the faithful.

His most celebrated contribution, the *Supplementum Summae Pisanellae* (also known as *Summa Astesana* in some contexts due to its association with similar works), was a comprehensive expansion of Bartolomeo da San Concordio's *Summa de casibus conscientiae*. Completed around 1444, this voluminous work addressed an exhaustive range of moral dilemmas, sins, and canonical regulations pertinent to the sacrament of penance. Beyond this magnum opus, Nicholas authored the *Quadriga spirituale*, a practical guide for spiritual life and confession, and the *Interrogatorium pro confessoribus*, providing structured questions for confessors to ascertain penitents' sins. These texts were not merely academic exercises but tools designed to standardize and rationalize pastoral care in an era of increasing lay piety and complex social changes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nicholas of Osimo's comprehensive moral theology manuals, particularly the *Supplementum Summae Pisanellae*, became standard reference works for confessors across Europe for over a century, profoundly shaping the practical application of Catholic moral teaching. His works were among the most frequently printed theological texts of the incunabula period, indicating their widespread and enduring impact on pastoral care.
